idiom_name: RequestContext struct threaded by reference, stack-allocated
implementation_notes: The classic form compiles directly: a RequestContext with typed accessors, created by a factory at the entry point and passed by reference (or pointer) to each layer, stack-allocated where possible so no allocation sits on the request path - TAO's CORBA ServerRequest context is the canonical high-performance example. Dependencies stay visible in the signature, the compiler sees through the accessors, and the lifetime is exactly the call stack; the framework-flavoured variants are only worth their indirection when the attribute set is not known at compile time.
pitfalls: A context stored in a member or captured by a long-lived callback outlives the frame it was allocated in - keep it on the request's stack or own it explicitly.
A virtual accessor per attribute costs a pointer chase on the hot path; prefer a plain struct with inline accessors passed by reference.

variants.name: std::any-keyed request registry
variants.idiom_name: std::any map with any_cast lookups (type-erased context)
variants.implementation_notes: For framework-style flows where the concrete attributes are decided by plugins, the context becomes a type-erased registry: one std::any per slot, written with emplace and read with any_cast<T>, so layers can add attributes without changing the context type. This trades compile-time knowledge of the context's shape for openness - a missing or mistyped slot surfaces as std::bad_any_cast at read time - so it suits middleware/interceptor stacks rather than a fixed request type.
pitfalls: any_cast throws std::bad_any_cast when the slot holds another type or is empty, so the registry must either pre-populate defaults or guard with has_value().
Type erasure hides which attributes exist: without a schema or a typed facade documenting the slots, the bag degrades into string-keyed globals with better error messages.

variants.name: thread_local ambient request slot bound by RAII
variants.idiom_name: thread_local RequestContext* with RAII bind/reset guard
variants.implementation_notes: Where the flow cannot take a parameter - callback-driven I/O, signal handlers, third-party code - the context pointer is parked in a thread_local slot and bound with an RAII guard that restores the previous value on scope exit. Each thread has its own instance for the lifetime of the thread, which is exactly the leak: the value is separated from the request's life, so pooled or reused threads must clear it. Keep this variant at the outermost boundary only; below it, pass the context explicitly.
pitfalls: The slot is per thread, not per request: with a worker pool the next request sees the last one's context unless the outermost guard clears it.
A context bound in one thread is invisible to work handed to another thread or to a coroutine resumed elsewhere, so asynchronous continuations silently read a null or stale pointer.
